list.listitem: Clinical presentation typically includes fever, myalgia, and classic rash. C
Chickenpox (varicella) and related complications are largely preventable with a two-dose vaccine series for healthy children and adolescents, A and for adults. C
Varicella vaccination is recommended for postexposure prophylaxis and outbreak control in susceptible healthy persons without contraindications. B

Varicella zoster immunoglobulin (VZIG) is recommended for postexposure prophylaxis in susceptible persons who are immunocompromised, pregnant, or at increased risk for severe disease but unable to receive vaccine. B
Give oral acyclovir within 24 hours for uncomplicated varicella in healthy patients over 12 years of age. B

background.definition: Varicella is a highly infectious disease caused by the varicella zoster virus (VZV). It is a systemic infection involving a characteristic itchy vesicular rash, aches, and fever. Significant complications including death occur rarely in healthy children and more often in neonates, adolescents, adults, pregnant women, and immunocompromised individuals.

list.listitem: During the prevaccination era (prior to introduction of varicella vaccine in 1995), an average of 4 million new cases of varicella were diagnosed each year in the United States.
It most commonly occurs in children younger than 10 years, with outbreaks most frequently occurring in the winter and spring.
Since the introduction of the varicella vaccine, varicella-related hospitalizations have dropped 75% to 100% depending on age group, and varicella-related deaths have dropped 86% as of 2003.
In Belgium, a country without universal vaccination, the rate of hospitalizations was 29.5/100,000 children, peaking between ages 0 and 4 years. Mortality was 0.5/1,000,000/year.
Similarly, in Sweden, another country without routine vaccination, the mortality rate was 0.34/1,000,000 person-years and the hospitalization rate was 35.6/1,000,000 person-years.
Indirect costs resulting from lost parental work productivity are responsible for 90% of the total costs of varicella illness.
Average hours of lost work productivity for parents of children with uncomplicated varicella disease in Canada vary by age of the child but range from 22.8 to 80.9 hours per ill child.
VZV, a double-stranded DNA virus of the herpesvirus family.
Spread by respiratory droplet transmission or contact with infectious secretions from vesicles.
Certain medications increase the risk of varicella zoster infections, such as fingolimod used in multiple sclerosis treatment.
The virus enters through respiratory or conjunctival mucosa and colonizes regional lymph nodes of the throat.
Primary viremia occurs 4 to 6 days after virus entry.
Replication occurs predominantly in the reticuloendothelial cells of the spleen and liver.
Immunity develops through humoral and T-cell pathways.
Give two doses of varicella vaccine to prevent chickenpox in healthy, nonpregnant, immunocompetent children A and in adults C who are not otherwise immune.
Immunize children routinely at the 12- to 15-month and the 4- to 6-year well child checks. A
Universal screening for susceptibility is recommended prenatally with postnatal vaccination. C

Give VZIG, 125 U/10 kg body weight, within 96 hours of exposure and as soon as possible for immunocompromised patients, pregnant women, neonates born to mothers who developed varicella from 5 days before to 2 days after giving birth, or exposed premature infants. B
To prevent one case of varicella, providers must vaccinate 6 to 12 individuals.
Screening for evidence of immunity is recommended in all pregnant women and health care personnel, regardless of year of birth.

Acceptable evidence of immunity includes documentation of vaccination, lab evidence of immunity, birth in the United States before 1980, and diagnosis or verification of varicella or herpes zoster by health care provider. See for criteria for health care provider immunity verification.

Give a two-dose series of varicella vaccination at 12 to 15 months and at 4 to 6 years for all children. The second dose is needed because immunity has been shown to wane after 5 years.The second dose can be given as early as 3 months after the first. The second dose does not need to be repeated if it is inadvertently given at least 28 days after the first. Use of the two dose regimen has been associated with a reduction in varicilla outbreaks.
Coverage is currently 92% at 2 years and 94% at entrance to kindergarten in the US.

Varicella vaccine is a live attenuated vaccine. Contraindications include malignancy, primary or acquired immunodeficiency, first-degree relative with congenital or hereditary immunodeficiency, or persons receiving high-dose immunosuppressive therapy, including oral steroids (>2 mg/kg or total of >20 mg/d of prednisone equivalent for more than 2 weeks). A systematic review from EULAR found insufficient evidence to draw definite conclusions about the safety of vaccination in children with rheumatic diseases.
Vaccine effectiveness is estimated to be at least 90%.
A meta-analysis concluded that vaccine effectiveness against moderate to severe varicella was 98% (95% CI 98% to 99%).

Nonpregnant women of child-bearing age who are vaccinated should avoid pregnancy for 1 month following vaccination. If a pregnant woman becomes vaccinated or a woman becomes pregnant within 1 month of vaccination, she should be counseled about potential effects on the fetus. The potential risk, if any, is low.

All susceptible adolescents and adults, including nonpregnant women of reproductive age, should be offered a two-shot series of varicella vaccination. Injections must be separated by at least 28 days. Revised guidelines recommend this for adults after 1980 without documented varicella infection or herpes zoster.
Two-dose vaccination is recommended for all health care personnel without adequate evidence of immunity () and is the preferred method for preventing varicella in health care settings.
Single-dose varicella vaccine is 85% effective at preventing varicella and over 95% effective at modifying severe disease in children.
Varicella vaccine has been combined with measles/mumps/rubella in a single vaccination (MMRV).

A report from the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) found 1.3 serious adverse events per 100,000 doses distributed for both varicella and MMRV vaccines between 2006 and 2020. Several deaths occurred in immunocompromised persons with absolute contraindications to the vaccine but who received it in error.
During the first 12 years following the initial single dose US vaccination program, deaths due to varicella decreased dramatically from 0.41 to 0.05 per million population.
Varicella vaccine is the intervention of choice for prevention of varicella after exposure in healthy and nonpregnant individuals above 1 year of age without evidence of immunity.
Vaccination within 3 days and 5 days is over 90% and 70% effective in preventing varicella, respectively. Both are 100% effective in modifying severe disease.

VariZIG is a varicella zoster immune globulin preparation approved for use in December, 2012. It is indicated as soon as possible after exposure to varicella for the immunocompromised groups listed in without evidence of immunity to varicella. It is most effective when given within 4 days of exposure.

Acyclovir should be given immediately in patients who received VariZIG if signs or symptoms of varicella disease occur. Patients receiving VariZIG should be observed closely for signs or symptoms of varicella for 28 days after exposure, as VariZIG might prolong the incubation period by more than 1 week.

To prevent subsequent varicella, patients receiving VariZIG should receive varicella vaccine 5 months after VariZIG administration, if not contraindicated. The vaccine is not needed if the patient has documented varicella disease after administration of VariZIG.
Acyclovir is not recommended for prophylactic use in healthy or immunocompromised persons.
Ribavirin is not effective for prevention of varicella in recent contacts.
Typical presentation includes fever, myalgia, and vesicular rash evolving to scabbed-over lesions, beginning centrally in crops and then proceeding outward. C
“Breakthrough varicella” (occurring more than 42 days after vaccination) is characterized by a more papular rash, low or no fever, milder symptoms overall, and a shorter course (4–6 days). C
Complications include secondary skin infections, pneumonia, cerebellar ataxia, or encephalitis, and death. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Characteristic lesions, exposure; both produce positive Tzanck stain, so culture or antibody test may be needed to distinguish them
Characteristic presentation, Tzanck stain, culture, or antibody serology
Dermatomal distribution in herpes zoster, versus diffuse distribution in varicella

list.listitem: Patients usually present with fever, myalgias, and rash.

Rash evolves from pruritic and maculopapular to vesicular lesions within hours; the rash begins centrally and progresses peripherally, and lesions appear in groups over time. Lesions usually crust or scab by day 5, but crusting may take longer in immunocompromised or other individuals. Uncrusted lesions are contagious. The rash generally appears about 15 days postexposure (range 11–21 days).

Signs or symptoms of complications: secondary skin infections such as impetigo and cellulitis, pneumonia (increased respiratory rate, auscultatory findings on pulmonary examination, respiratory distress in severe cases), and CNS changes such as ataxia or mental status changes as a result of cerebellar ataxia or encephalitis.

In breakthrough varicella (individuals vaccinated more than 42 days before presentation of first symptoms), the rash is more likely to be predominantly maculopapular rather than vesicular and is still contagious.
Routine use of diagnostic testing is not recommended. Confirmation of infection is available with viral culture of lesion drainage or elevated IgM serum assays.
Tzanck smear of vesicular fluid looking for multinucleated giant cells may assist in diagnosis but is only specific to a virus in the herpes family.
ELISA tests to VZV-specific envelope glycoproteins (gp) and whole antigen extract from VZV-infected cells are sensitive and specific for VZVIG and can reliably indicate varicella immune status.

To exclude VZV vasculopathy, the diagnostic value of CSF anti-VZVIG is greater than that of CSF VZV DNA (done more quickly by PCR). Negative results for both tests are required to rule out vasculopathy.
CSF can be collected for viral culture, ELISA for varicella antibodies, and viral DNA for PCR in patients with symptoms suggestive of encephalitis or varicella vasculopathy.
Clinical diagnosis based on history and physical examination is acceptable for almost all diagnoses of varicella, and laboratory testing is unnecessary in most patients.
In confusing cases, or when signs or symptoms of varicella complications are present, diagnostic testing may be appropriate.
CSF can be collected for viral culture, ELISA for varicella antibodies, and viral DNA for PCR in patients with symptoms suggestive of encephalitis or varicella vasculopathy.

Oral acyclovir is recommended within 24 hours of rash for healthy persons over 12 years of age with typical varicella disease (20 mg/kg orally up to a maximum dose of 800 mg, four times daily for 5 days). B
Oral acyclovir should be considered in healthy patients with typical varicella and increased risk of severe varicella. C
IV acyclovir is indicated for treatment of varicella disease in immunocompromised individuals and those with severe complications. C
For symptomatic treatment of fever and aches, acetaminophen should be considered. Aspirin is contraindicated due to the risk of Reye’s syndrome. C

Oral acyclovir treatment (20 mg/kg, up to a maximum of 800 mg, by mouth four times daily for 5 days) reduces the number of lesions (mean 76 lesions, range 8-145) and duration of fever (about 1 day), but has no effect on complication rates or rates of disease transmission.
Oral acyclovir should be started within 24 hours of rash onset and continued for 5 days in healthy patients over 12 years old with typical chickenpox.
Children taking salicylates who develop varicella should be given acyclovir. Oral acyclovir should also be considered in other individuals with risk for severe varicella.
Acyclovir is of uncertain necessity for healthy children under 12 years of age with typical varicella and without specific risk for severe varicella.
IV acyclovir should be used in immunocompromised patients with systemic disease (10 mg/kg every 8 hours for 7 days).
Supportive treatments may be considered, including antihistamines, calamine lotion, Aveeno baths for pruritus, and acetaminophen for fever.
Aspirin should be avoided due to its association with Reye’s syndrome.
Clip fingernails to decrease trauma and scarring from itching, especially for younger children.
Admit patients to the ICU if they have altered consciousness, seizures, ataxia, or respiratory distress.
Treat all newborns for varicella exposure with IVIG whose mothers developed varicella less than 5 days before or within 2 days after delivery; also monitor them closely for signs of disease.
The most common complications in children are secondary skin infections (ie, impetigo, cellulitis, or erysipelas) with group A streptococcus and Staphylococcus aureus organisms (5%–10%).

Suspect secondary infection when skin manifestations do not improve in 3 to 4 days, fever returns or worsens, or the clinical condition deteriorates after initial improvement. Obtain skin cultures before starting empiric antibiotic therapy.

Pneumonia is the most common complication in adolescents and adults (1 in 400) and can be fatal. Respiratory symptoms usually begin 3 to 4 days after rash appears. Treat with IV acyclovir and supportive therapy.
CNS sequelae most commonly include acute postinfectious cerebellar ataxia (1 of 4000 patients with varicella).

Encephalitis occurs in 1.7 patients per 100,000 cases in otherwise healthy children between the ages of 1 year and 14 years. Treat with IV acyclovir, supportive therapy, and specialty referral as appropriate.
Herpes zoster occurs months to years after primary infection in about 15% of patients.
Case series of adults with varicella pneumonia suggest a possible benefit to corticosteroids.
Supportive care, in the hospital or ICU as needed, potentially includes ventilation and specialty consultation and treatment.
Acyclovir IV is usually recommended.

In hospital settings, exposed susceptible individuals should be isolated beginning 10 days after the first exposure, until 21 days after the last exposure (or 28 days after the last exposure if given VZIG).
The disease is typically self-limited, with low morbidity and mortality in healthy children; it can last up to 21 days. C
Most severe disease occurs in adults, adolescents, immunocompromised patients, and neonates born from 5 days after to 2 days before onset of symptoms in their mothers. C
Breakthrough disease is generally milder, with reduced risk of severe complications. B
Anorexia and headache are generally mild in children but can be significant in adolescents and adults.
Disease in vaccinated individuals is less likely to cause complications and is less contagious than disease in unvaccinated individuals.
After primary infection, the virus remains dormant in nervous tissue; reactivation later in life presents as herpes zoster.
Clinical and subclinical reinfections are more common than previously thought, although still rare.
Individuals may be contagious before symptoms occur, so isolation may not prevent all transmission.
Varicella disease is usually self-limited in healthy children, with low morbidity and mortality.
Neonates born to mothers with signs and symptoms of varicella 5 days before to 2 days after delivery have a mortality rate of up to 30%.
Older infants are usually mildly affected.
Severe disease with complications is more likely to occur in adults, adolescents, preterm neonates, and immunocompromised individuals.
Prior to introduction of VariZIG, children with leukemia had a mortality rate of 7% from varicella disease. It is now less than 1%.
See for recommendations on furlough from work for health care personnel.
Children should be excluded from school and other public gathering places for 5 days after onset of rash, or until all lesions have scabbed.
Skin lesions may take longer to scab in immunocompromised individuals or those on steroids.
Screening for evidence of immunity is recommended in all pregnant women. Pregnant women seronegative for VZV who are exposed to chickenpox should be given VZIG.
Birth before 1980 alone is not sufficient evidence of immunity. See .
Pregnant women who are seronegative should be educated about avoiding exposure, obtaining care if exposure occurs, and the importance of postdelivery vaccination.
Varicella vaccination is not contraindicated in breastfeeding.
Women who develop varicella during pregnancy are at risk for fetal congenital varicella syndrome, with greatest risk (2%) when infection occurs at 13 to 20 weeks of gestation.
The likelihood of adverse consequences if varicella vaccine is inadvertently given to a pregnant woman is low.

feature.caption: Specific Recommendations for Health Care Personnel (HCP) Regarding Varicella.
feature.feature_body: CDC Recommendations for HCP (2007) All HCP must demonstrate evidence of immunity to varicella: Birth in the United States before 1980 is not considered to be evidence of immunity. If no history of varicella, HCP should receive a two-dose vaccination. Serologic screening before vaccination of HCP with negative or uncertain history of varicella is probably cost effective. Routine testing after two-dose vaccination of HCP is unnecessary. Secondary prevention of HCP after exposure to varicella: If HCP have received one dose of varicella vaccine, they need to receive a second dose within 3–5 days after exposure to rash (providing 4 weeks have elapsed since first vaccine dose). If HCP have received two doses of varicella vaccine, they should be monitored daily during days 10–21 postexposure to determine clinical status. Unvaccinated HCP with no evidence of immunity exposed to VZV should receive postexposure varicella vaccination as soon as possible; they are potentially infective from days 10–21 postexposure and should be furloughed during this period.

feature.caption: Indications for the Use of Varicella Zoster Immunoglobulin (VZIG or VariZIG).
feature.feature_body: Administer VZIG as soon as possible after exposure to the following groups if there is no evidence of varicella immunity: Pregnant women Neonates born to mothers with signs and symptoms of varicella 5 days before to 2 days after the time of delivery Hospitalized premature infants born at 28+ weeks gestation whose mothers do not have evidence of immunity to varicella Hospitalized premature infants born at <28 weeks gestation or who weigh ≤1000 gm at birth, regardless of their. mother's evidence of immunity to varicella Immunocompromised children and adults, including: Those with HIV/AIDs Those with malignancies (eg, leukemia, lymphoma) Those on high-dose steroid therapy defined as the equivalent of >2 mg/kg or total of >20 mg/d of prednisone equivalent for >2 weeks
